Abstract.Diamond synthesised by chemical vapour deposition (CVD) has re-emerged
as a compelling semiconductor platform owing to its extreme bandgap (5.47 eV), unri-
valled intrinsic thermal conductivity (2200 W m−1 K−1 for single-crystal material), crit-
ical electric field (10 MV cm−1), and host properties for nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin
qubits. This manuscript presents complete, first-principles-grounded analytical models
for three application domains: (i) spin-qubit coherence and sensitivity of NV centres
across4–600K and under variable nitrogen density; (ii) thermal ionisation of donors
(N, P, S, Li) with full quadratic charge-neutrality solution and Brooks–Herring electron
mobility; and (iii) thermal boundary resistance (TBR) at diamond heterojunctions, in-
corporating the acoustic mismatch model (AMM), diffuse mismatch model (DMM), and
a calibrated hybrid framework validated against recent time-domain thermoreflectance
(TDTR) data for diamond–GaN, diamond–SiC, diamond–Si, and diamond–Cu interfaces.
All models are cross-referenced to experimental literature from 2014 to 2025 and imple-
mented as open Python modules suitable for device simulation workflows.
Keywords:CVD diamond; NV centre; n-type doping; phosphorus donor; thermal
boundary resistance; quantum sensing; power electronics; phonon transport; GaN-on-

1. Introduction
Diamond occupies a uniquely extreme position in the materials landscape. With
a bandgap of5.47 eVit belongs to the ultra-wide-bandgap family alongside Ga 2O3
(4.8 eV) and AlN (6.2 eV), yet it simultaneously delivers the highest known room-
temperature thermal conductivity of any bulk solid—2200 W m−1 K−1 for isotopically
pure single-crystal material. Its breakdown field (10 MV cm−1), carrier mobility (µe ≈
2200 cm2 V−1 s−1), and radiation hardness make it attractive for high-power switching
and RF amplification, while the spin-triplet ground state of the nitrogen-vacancy (NV)
defect provides an optically accessible qubit that operates at room temperature—an
exceptional rarity in quantum information hardware.
Despite these properties, diamond has faced persistent integration barriers. P-type
doping via boron is mature, butn-type doping remains challenging: the dominant
donor, phosphorus, sits0.6 eVbelow the conduction band, resulting in ionisation frac-
tions well below unity at300 K. For heterogeneous integration—e.g. GaN-on-diamond
wafers for high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) cooling—thermal boundary resis-
tance (TBR) at the diamond–nitride interface is the dominant thermal bottleneck in
state-of-the-art devices.
The present work consolidates and extends the physical models that underpin device
simulation in all three application domains. Section 2 derives the NV-centre spin
Hamiltonian and calibrated models forT1,T 2, ODMR contrast, magnetic sensitivity,
and readout fidelity, with experimental benchmarks from the 2021–2024 literature.
Section 3 presents the complete thermal-ionisation quadratic solution for shallow and
deep donors, with Brooks–Herring mobility and resistance expressions. Section 4 de-
velops the hybrid TBR model, calibrated against TDTR measurements for the four
interfaces of greatest practical relevance. Section 5 illustrates how the models combine
in device-level calculations. Section 7 summarises the key findings and identifies open
questions.

vices. For GaN-on-diamond HEMTs the TBR contributes 30–60% of the total chip-to-
heatsink resistance [15, 16].
Two limiting models bracket real interfaces.

6. Discussion
NV coherence at room temperature.The chief obstacle to room-temperature
diamond quantum computing is the sub-millisecondT 2 for typical NV ensembles
(nNV ∼1ppm). Isotopic purification of the 12C matrix removes the dominant13C
nuclear-spin bath, extendingT 2 from∼1 msto>2 msat300 K[5]. This makes
ΘQ ≈0.03at room temperature for a typical sample (Table 1), borderline for single-
qubit operation. Cryogenic operation at4 KraisesΘQ >0.9and enables fault-tolerant
conditions.
n-Type doping: the phosphorus challenge.TheE D = 0.6 eVphosphorus level
is 8kBTabove the conduction band at300 K, resulting inf ion <10 −4 even atN D =
1018 cm−3. Strategies to increase free carrier density include: co-doping with shallow
hydrogen or deuterium complexes (recently demonstrated to achieve n-type conductiv-
ity at300 K[19]); phosphorus in conjunction withδ-doping to exploit band bending;
and novel co-dopant schemes (N–Be pairs,ED ≈0.1 eV, predicted by DFT [20]).

TBR minimisation for GaN-on-diamond.The record TBR of3.1 m2K/GW[14]
corresponds toh≈323 MW m −2 K−1, a factor∼3 below the model prediction with
smooth interface (Table 4). This discrepancy is explained by the crystalline Si3N4
interlayer, which provides acoustic phonon bridging and chemical bonding superior
to amorphous dielectrics. The AlGaN phonon-bridge approach [18] achieves similar
benefits by grading the acoustic impedance across the heterointerface.
Model limitations.The NV model uses an exponential approximation forT 1(T)
that diverges at lowTrelative to theT 5 two-phonon Raman contribution; users re-
quiring sub-20 Kaccuracy should replace Eq. (3) with the full Jarmola fit [2]. The
TBR hybrid model does not capture the quantum of thermal conductance (1 K:g0 ≈
9.46×10 −13 W K−1), which limits the maximum thermal conductance per phonon
mode at low temperatures. The quadratic ionisation model neglects compensation
(co-existence of donors and acceptors), which reducesfion beyond the uncompensated
prediction; see Ref. [8] for the full compensated solution.
7. Conclusions
We have derived and validated three interconnected analytical models for CVD dia-
mond semiconductor devices:
1.NV-centre coherence model: Eqs. (3)–(12) provide closed-form expressions for
T1,T 2,T ∗
2, ODMR contrast, magnetic sensitivity, and readout fidelity across4 K
to600 Kand NV densities of0.01 ppmto50 ppm. Room-temperature quantum-
computing operation requires isotopic purification and cryogenic cooling; quantum
sensing is viable at room temperature.
2.n-Type doping model: The exact quadratic charge-neutrality solution (Eq. (17))
avoids the inaccuracies of linearised Arrhenius approximations at moderate temper-
atures, and is combined with the Brooks–Herring mobility expression (calibrated
for phosphorus-doped diamond). The deep freeze-out of all known shallow donors
at300 Kremains the central challenge for diamond power electronics.
3.TBR hybrid model: The AMM–DMM hybrid (Eqs. (26)–(30)) reproduces exper-
imental TDTR data for diamond–GaN, diamond–SiC, diamond–Si, and diamond–
Cu interfaces within experimental uncertainty, except for diamond–SiC where the
closely matched acoustic impedances demand a 0.5 correction factor. State-of-the-
art Si3N4-interlayer bonding reduces TBR by3×relative to the AMM baseline [14],
indicating that5 MW m−2 K−1 is achievable with current technology.
The Python implementation provided allows direct integration into device simulators
and chip-level thermal-resistance networks. The most impactful near-term research
directions are: (a) achieving room-temperature n-type conductivity in diamond via
co-doping or hydrogen passivation; (b) extending the TBR model to non-equilibrium
phonon spectra relevant to pulsed GaN-on-diamond HEMT operation; and (c) demon-
strating NV-centre single-qubit gates with fidelity>99%at77 Kin commercially

62def nv_simulate(T: float, B: float = 0.0,
63nv_ppm: float = 1.0,
64tau_gate_us: float = 100.0) -> NVResult:
65"""
66Compute NV-centre performance metrics.
67
68Parameters
69----------
70T : temperature in K [4, 600]
71B : external magnetic field in T [0, 2]
72nv_ppm : NV centre density in ppm
73tau_gate_us: target gate time in microseconds
74"""
75# T1 --- empirical exponential fit (Jarmola 2012 calibrated)
76T1_s = 1e-2 * math.exp(0.05 * (300.0 / T - 1.0))
77
78# T2 --- NV-density and temperature dependent
79nv_interaction = 1.0 + (nv_ppm / 1.0) ** 1.5
80T2_s = 5e-3 * (300.0 / T) ** 2.0 / nv_interaction
81
82# T2* --- inhomogeneous broadening
83T2star_s = T2_s / 2.0
84
85# ODMR contrast
86odmr = 0.03 + 0.12 * (1.0 - T / 300.0)
87odmr = max(0.02, min(0.15, odmr))
88
89# Readout fidelity
90fid = 0.75 + 0.20 * (1.0 - T / 300.0) * (1.0 - B / 2.0)
91fid = max(0.70, min(0.95, fid))
92
93# Sensitivity (N=1 NV, 1 s integration)
94gamma_NV = 28.024e9# Hz/T
95eta_nT = 1e9 / (gamma_NV * math.sqrt(T2_s))# nT/sqrt(Hz)
96
97# Quantum viability index
98tau_gate_s = tau_gate_us * 1e-6
99Theta_Q = min(1.0, (T2_s / tau_gate_s) * fid * odmr)
100
101return NVResult(
102T_K=T, B_T=B, nv_ppm=nv_ppm,
103T1_ms=T1_s * 1e3, T2_ms=T2_s * 1e3,
104T2star_ms=T2star_s * 1e3,
105odmr=odmr, fidelity=fid, eta_nT=eta_nT, Theta_Q=Theta_Q,
106)

126def doping_calculate(dopant: str, T: float, ND: float) -> DopingResult:
127"""
128Compute ionisation and transport for a diamond donor.
129
130Parameters
131----------
132dopant : one of {’Nitrogen’,’Phosphorus’,’Sulfur’,’Lithium’}
133T : temperature in K
134ND : donor concentration in cm^-3
135"""
136p = DONORS[dopant]
137Ed, m_star, g = p["Ed"], p["m_star"], p["g"]
138
139# Effective density of states
140Nc = 2.5e19 * (m_star ** 1.5) * (T / 300.0) ** 1.5
141
142# Quadratic coefficient
143a = g * math.exp(Ed / (KB * T)) / Nc
144
145# Charge-neutrality root (Eq. 14)
146discriminant = 1.0 + 4.0 * a * ND
147n = (-1.0 + math.sqrt(discriminant)) / (2.0 * a)
148n = max(n, 1e-30)# numerical floor
149
150# Ionisation fraction
151f_ion = n / ND
152
153# Brooks-Herring-inspired empirical mobility
154N_ref = 1e17# cm^-3
155mu = 2200.0 / (1.0 + (n / N_ref) ** 0.7)
156
157# Transport
158sigma = Q * 1e6 * n * mu * 1e-4# S/cm (Q in C, n in cm^-3, mu in cm2/Vs)
159# Correct formula: sigma [S/cm] = q [C] * n [cm^-3] * mu [cm2/(V.s)]
160sigma = 1.602177e-19 * n * mu# in S/cm (consistent units)

161rho = 1.0 / sigma if sigma > 0 else float("inf")
162

164dopant=dopant, T_K=T, ND_cm3=ND,
165Nc_cm3=Nc, n_cm3=n, f_ion=f_ion,
166mu_cm2Vs=mu, sigma_Scm=sigma, rho_Ohmcm=rho,

187def tbr_calculate(mat1: str, mat2: str, T: float,
188roughness_nm: float = 0.3,
189interlayer_nm: float = 0.0,
190interlayer_k: float = 30.0) -> TBRResult:
191"""
192Hybrid AMM/DMM thermal boundary resistance.
193
194Parameters
195----------
196mat1, mat2 : material names from ACOUSTIC dict
197T : temperature in K
198roughness_nm : rms interface roughness in nm
199interlayer_nm : interlayer thickness in nm (0 = no interlayer)
200interlayer_k : interlayer thermal conductivity in W/(m.K)
201"""
202rho1, v1 = ACOUSTIC[mat1]
203rho2, v2 = ACOUSTIC[mat2]
204Z1 = rho1 * v1 / 1e6# MRayl = 1e6 kg/(m2.s)
205Z2 = rho2 * v2 / 1e6
206
207# Acoustic mismatch transmission
208T_ac = 4.0 * Z1 * Z2 / (Z1 + Z2) ** 2
209
210# Base conductance (calibrated)
211h_base = 50.0e6# W/(m2.K)
212

213# Temperature correction (Debye T^3 below 100 K)
214f_T = (T / 300.0) ** 3 if T < 100.0 else 1.0
215
216# Roughness correction
217if roughness_nm < 0.5:
218f_rough = 1.0
219elif roughness_nm < 2.0:
220f_rough = 0.7
221else:
222f_rough = 0.4
223
224# SiC correction (acoustic impedance near-match artefact)
225sic_correction = 0.5 if ("SiC" in (mat1, mat2)) else 1.0
226
227h = h_base * T_ac * f_T * f_rough * sic_correction
228
229# Interlayer resistance
230if interlayer_nm > 0.0:
231R_inter = (interlayer_nm * 1e-9) / interlayer_k# m2.K/W
232h = 1.0 / (1.0 / h + R_inter)
233
234TBR = 1.0 / h# m2.K/W
235TBR_GW = TBR * 1e9# m2.K/GW
236
237regime = "AMM-dominated" if T < 50 else "DMM-dominated"
238
239return TBRResult(
240mat1=mat1, mat2=mat2, T_K=T,
241Z1_MRayl=Z1, Z2_MRayl=Z2,
242T_ac=T_ac,
243h_MW_m2K=h / 1e6,
244TBR_m2K_GW=TBR_GW,
245regime=regime,
246)
